newsitem.title: UK: SUGAR - EU demand slackens, availability adequate.
newsitem.headline: SUGAR - EU demand slackens, availability adequate.

text.p: Demand for European Union (EU) white sugars has dwindled and the usual perception of summer tightness now appears to be without foundation, European physical brokers said on Friday.

But availability was artificially reduced as much of the sugar remaining from the EU's 1996/97 crop was either being retained by producers or already bought up and stored by major trade houses, they said.
While there is no shortage of offers for EU sugars bids have been few and far between. "There's been very little trading," said one broker.
Premiums for prompt cargoes were quoted at around $9.00 over August futures for shipment ex-Antwerp and $7.50 from elsewhere.

Both quotes were for packing in polypropylene bags, for which London's LIFFE exchange will make an allowance with physical deliveries against futures expiries from August 1998 when a discount of $6 per tonne will apply.
Traders said the EU premiums were little changed in recent weeks as few purchases were being concluded.

But it has been suggested for some time that some holders of European sugars could be keeping a tight rein on supply in response to the weakened demand and also to ensure that premiums remained supported.
"There's still a lot around but it's being held in very tight hands," said another broker.

"Producers have got sugar -- but if you want to go into the market and buy some, it's not easy. If you want to buy two or three cargoes it's a bit of a scrape to get it together but you do eventually," he said.
Some traders are reported to be offering EU sugars for nearby shipment at cheaper prices than usual just in order to relieve stock pressure.

Europe's summer months are traditionally a time of supply tightness as the period falls in between the tail-end of the current season's crop but is still before the autumn harvesting of the next season's beets.
Futures traders normally try to avoid taking short August positions to avoid a price squeeze and having to find sugar at expiry.
Two years ago, for example, the summer tightness caused a massive squeeze on the shorts and the physical EU premium rocketed to as much as $160 over October.
Some of the sugar already bought and held by major players had yet to be placed as homes were hard to find -- and not only for European sugar.
Traders cited one leading European operator with a hefty stockpile of Brazilian 100 ICUMSA sugars.
While 45 ICUMSA cargoes are available from Brazil and Thailand, there was more interest in lesser-quality sugars -- but even these were being offered cheaply.
Brazil ICUMSA cargoes were quoted at discounts of between $10 and $12 to London's August contract.
As far as the EU's quotas are concerned, more C sugar is thought be in supply. C sugar is produced over and above member states' normal production quotas and is destined for world export markets.
"I think there's more C sugar around than A or B," said one trader. "They (producers) have got rid of what they want to get rid of and they'll carry the C sugar forward. A lot will be rolled."
More A and B sugars had stayed in the EU's internal market this year, he said, citing exchange trades between Germany and Italy as an example. This had reduced Germany's world market exports.
"Unless something new comes out, I think most traders are close to covering all their requirements," he said.
-- Jeremy Smith, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
